transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what’s been bothering you or what brings you in today?

Hi, doctor. Thanks for seeing me. 

Well, what brings me in is... I just keep getting stuck on this issue with my face. It's this sagging, uneven look around my jaw and on one side of my face. I really started fixating on it after seeing myself in a bunch of recent family photos, and now I just can't seem to unsee it. 

The thing is, my wife says she barely notices anything at all. And I work as a financial advisor, so I'm face-to-face with people all day, and my clients don't seem to notice it either. But... it's just really bothering me, and I can't stop focusing on how uneven it looks.
Have you found yourself avoiding certain social situations, work interactions, or activities because you're self-conscious about the way your face looks?

Well, I still get through my work. But... I have noticed I've been a bit slower getting out the door for client meetings lately. And during some of those appointments, I'm probably a little less present than I should be, just because it's on my mind. 

Outside of work, yeah, I guess I have avoided a few things. I've skipped a few art openings my wife and I usually go to. I just... I didn't really want to be seen, or have to worry about being photographed again.
Do you find yourself spending a lot of time thinking about this facial asymmetry, or does it cause you a significant amount of distress?

Yeah, I do spend a lot of time thinking about it. It's hard to put an exact number on it, but it crosses my mind pretty frequently throughout the day. It's definitely distressing to me. Like I said, it's distracting me at work and making me want to skip things I usually enjoy. I just feel really uncomfortable about it.
Do you find yourself being preoccupied with other aspects of your appearance, beyond just the facial asymmetry, such as skin texture, hair, or other features?

No, not really. It's... it's really just the jaw and the unevenness on that side of my face. I don't really think twice about my hair or my skin or anything like that. It's just this one specific area that I can't seem to get past.
Have you found yourself doing anything repeatedly, like checking mirrors, touching your face, or trying to cover it up, because of how you feel about the asymmetry?

Yeah, I do. Especially right before client meetings. I'll... I usually go check the bathroom mirror, and then I end up checking my phone camera several times, too. I try to adjust the lighting or maybe fix my collar, just trying to figure out the best way to angle my face so it's less noticeable. 

And then, even when I'm around people, I catch myself comparing my face to theirs. Like the younger advisors at the firm, or the guys at those gallery events I mentioned. I just sort of fixate on it, and I end up doing that instead of actually focusing on the conversation like I should be.

Do you feel that these thoughts about your face are intrusive or unwanted, and do they lead you to do things repeatedly, like checking mirrors or adjusting your appearance, to try to reduce your anxiety?

Yeah, they are definitely unwanted. I don't want to be thinking about my jaw when I should be working or, you know, talking to someone. It just kind of pops into my head. And like I said, yeah, I do check the mirror and my phone camera a lot, and I try to adjust how I'm standing or sitting to hide it. Doing that makes me feel a little better in the moment, I guess, but it doesn't really stop the thoughts from coming back.
Have you ever felt like these thoughts about your face are irrational or exaggerated, even though you can’t seem to stop having them?

I don't know if I'd say they're completely irrational, because I can see the unevenness when I look in the mirror. It's really there. But I do think... maybe I focus on it more than other people do? Like, I know it probably shouldn't take up this much of my time or energy, but I just can't seem to turn it off. So, I guess I know it's a bit exaggerated in my own head, even if the flaw itself is real.
Would you say that the unevenness on your face is something most people wouldn’t even notice, or do you think it’s something that stands out a lot to others?

Well, that's kind of what brought me in here to begin with. I keep getting stuck on this sagging, uneven look around my jaw and the one side of my face. It really started bothering me after seeing myself in a bunch of family photos recently. But... if I'm being honest, my wife says she barely notices anything. And my clients don't seem to notice either. So, I guess to other people it doesn't stand out a lot, but to me, it's all I can see.
Has this concern about your face gotten to the point where it interferes with your ability to function normally in your daily life, such as at work, socially, or in other important areas?

Well, I still get through my work. I'm getting my job done. But I will say I've been a lot slower getting out the door for client meetings lately, just checking the mirror and all that. And I've definitely been less present during some of those appointments, like my mind is just somewhere else instead of on their finances. 

Socially... yeah, it's getting in the way a bit. I've actually skipped a few art openings recently that my wife and I usually go to. I just... I really didn't want to be seen, or, you know, risk being photographed. So it is interfering, yeah.
Would you say that the unevenness on your face is something most people wouldn’t even notice, or do you think it’s something that stands out a lot to others?

I think we actually just touched on this a minute ago. But, um... yeah, most people probably don't notice it at all. Like I mentioned, my wife says she doesn't really see anything, and none of my clients have ever pointed it out. So I guess it doesn't stand out to anyone else, it's just... really obvious to me when I look in the mirror.

Do these concerns about your face feel more like something you can’t stop thinking about, or something you’re trying to prevent from getting worse by doing things like checking the mirror or adjusting your appearance?

It's a bit of both, but I definitely do a lot of checking and adjusting. Like I mentioned earlier about being slow to get out the door... before client meetings, I’ll go check the bathroom mirror, and then I'll pull out my phone camera several times just to see how it looks. 

I try to manage it by adjusting the lighting in the room if I can, or I'll change how my shirt collar sits, or try to keep my face angled a certain way so the sagging isn't as obvious. And it's not just the checking. I also catch myself constantly comparing my face to other people. I'll be looking at the younger advisors at the firm, or the guys at those gallery events, just comparing my jawline to theirs instead of actually focusing on the conversation I'm supposed to be having.

Do you find yourself performing any repetitive behaviors or mental acts, such as mirror checking, comparing your face to others, or mentally analyzing how you look, in response to your concerns about facial asymmetry?

Yeah, I think I actually just mentioned a lot of that, but... yes, I definitely do. Like I was just saying, right before my client meetings, I’ll check the bathroom mirror, and then I'll look at my phone camera several times. I do things like adjust the lighting in the room, maybe change how my collar sits, or try to angle my face a certain way so it doesn't look as uneven. 

And then with the mental stuff... yeah, I catch myself doing exactly that. I'll be comparing my face to the younger advisors at my firm, or the people at those gallery events, instead of actually focusing on the conversation I'm supposed to be having.
How much time per day would you say you spend thinking about or dealing with concerns about your facial asymmetry?

I'm not really sure, to be honest. I've never actually timed it or tried to add it all up. It's not like it takes over my entire day, but... it's definitely scattered throughout. 

It's a few minutes here when I'm getting ready, or checking my phone before a client meeting, and then maybe some time spent comparing myself when I'm out at an event. If I had to put a total number of hours on it, I really don't know what it would be. It just sort of happens in short bursts depending on what I'm doing that day.
